summary: Dr Sahebkar says a retraction is not a single verdict on a paper: notices range from fabricated data to duplicate publication, authorship disputes or a problem in one figure unrelated to the result being cited, and COPE guidance recommends citing retracted work with its status clearly marked. Whether a citation is a problem depends on whether the reason for retraction touches the statement it supports and whether the citing paper's conclusion rests on it, which a count of citations cannot answer. All seven papers in our letter are reviews of hundreds of sources, and he says none of their conclusions depends on the retracted papers. He asks that authors be compared by rates normalised by their total publications and cited references, not ranked by absolute counts, since a ranking by count is led by the authors who publish most. He was given the opportunity to send a direct response for publication instead of this summary.
our_response: Two of his points changed the lists for every author: the author list now shows a rate beside each count (for him, 6 of 144 papers, 4.2%), and citations of work retracted for reasons that do not touch its results are left out. The ranking stays by count, as set out in advance, and the rate counts papers, not references.
changes_since_letter: Every author: a rate is shown beside the count (papers citing retracted work as support, out of the author's open-access papers in PMC tagged with their ORCID iD, 2010 to 2026). | Every list: citations of work retracted only for reasons that do not touch the results are left out. Two of his items came off: Zhang P et al. (J Exp Clin Cancer Res 2017; the notice concerns the welfare of the mice and ethics approval) and Wu L et al. (Cell Biol Int; a signed copyright transfer agreement was not provided). | His entry: from 7 papers and 11 citations in our letter to 6 papers and 9 citations, all in reviews.

summary: Dr Nabavi checked the references and passages and accepts that the cited studies have retraction notices and are cited in support of statements in her reviews, but says this does not by itself show prior awareness, misconduct, or that the reviews' overall conclusions are invalid. She notes that her oxaliplatin review was submitted on 21 September 2023, before the cited circPTK2 study was retracted on 18 October 2023, though it was revised and published afterwards. She would need to review the manuscript history before giving an account of awareness, and is willing to work with her co-authors and the journals to assess the affected statements and pursue appropriate corrections. She asked that her entry be deferred until she has seen and answered the human check's findings, and that her response be published alongside her entry; it is printed below as she wrote it.
quote: Citation counts alone cannot establish that an entire review is unreliable.
statement:
Thank you for contacting me before publication and providing an opportunity to respond. I take the accuracy of the scientific record seriously.

I have checked the identified references and their surrounding passages. I acknowledge that the listed studies have retraction notices and are cited in support of scientific statements in the reviews. However, this does not, by itself, establish prior awareness of the retractions, individual misconduct, or that the reviews’ overall conclusions are invalid.

The publication timeline requires context. The oxaliplatin review was submitted on 21 September 2023, before the cited circPTK2 study was retracted on 18 October 2023, although the review was revised and published afterward. Please reflect this distinction in your account.

It is also important to distinguish the status of a review from that of a study it cites. For example, the May 2022 correction to “The long and short non-coding RNAs modulating EZH2 signaling in cancer” concerned a co-author’s name; it was not a retraction of that review. I recognise that this correction does not resolve the separate issue of its cited sources.

Regarding prior awareness, I would need to review the manuscript history and relevant correspondence before providing an accurate account for each citation. Assessing the effect on the reviews’ conclusions likewise requires examining the particular claims and the remaining evidence. Citation counts alone cannot establish that an entire review is unreliable. I remain willing to work with the co-authors and journals to assess the affected statements and pursue appropriate corrections.

I also have concerns about the opportunity afforded to authors to respond to editorial decisions. In some instances involving our own papers, my understanding is that we were notified only after retraction and were not given a meaningful opportunity to respond beforehand. This is a separate concern from the status of the studies cited in those papers.

Regarding the separate Elsevier retraction matter, I continue to disagree strongly with the decision and dispute the grounds provided. In our correspondence with Elsevier, we explained our position that the identified reference mismatches and Table 3 error could be addressed through a formal correction without invalidating the review’s overall conclusions. We supplied proposed corrections and requested a specific explanation of why a correction was considered insufficient. In our view, those concerns were not adequately addressed.

Please distinguish this disputed editorial matter from your citation analysis. If you discuss it, please accurately record that the authors disagree with the retraction and dispute its grounds.

I appreciate your clarification that your analysis concerns citation use rather than intent. Please preserve that distinction in the published presentation. As your figures remain provisional and human verification is pending, please provide the completed human-review findings when available. I request that publication of my individual entry be deferred until I have had a reasonable opportunity to review and respond to those findings.

I would welcome publication of this response alongside any summary concerning me, so that readers can consider my position in context.
our_response: Her dates are exact, and the timeline is printed beside that citation; it stays counted, because every entry is measured by the paper as published. We did not defer her entry, since the list is published whole. If she shows that a reading is wrong, we correct the entry and say so here.

(Bioengineered 2022): submitted 21 Sep 2023, before the retraction of 18 Oct 2023; revised, accepted and published (1 Dec 2023) after it. | Xie P et al. entry: A Comprehensive Review on Metabolic Syndrome
summary: Dr Kaur acknowledges that her 2014 review has been retracted and should not be relied on as an authoritative source; anyone who wants its summary figures or claims should consult the original publications and verify the evidence themselves. She notes that the publisher's notice found substantial material from earlier publications used mostly without citation, and that it records her apology for unintentionally leaving out most of the sources and her disagreement with the retraction. She asked that our explanation reflect the circumstances in the notice, alongside any broader category Retraction Watch uses.
quote: I acknowledge that the article has been retracted and should not be relied upon as an authoritative source.
our_response: We changed the reason to the notice's wording, which does not allege fabrication. Under a rule since applied to every entry, a paper retracted for reasons that do not touch its results is not listed, so her paper is not named on the page; it stays in the downloadable data with the notice's reason.

summary: Dr Hamblin says he has never knowingly cited a retracted paper and finds it hard to believe that anyone would. The papers in our letter all came from his collaborators in Iran, where internet access is sporadic, unreliable and slow, so researchers build a reference library when they have access and write from it later; a paper retracted after the library was built would not show as retracted, which he says explains our findings. He said none of these citations contains the word "retracted", though our letter said one reference list marked a work retracted.
quote: I have never knowingly cited a retracted paper and frankly I find it difficult to believe that anybody would knowingly do this
our_response: He was right about the one item our letter marked: its reference carries a link to the retraction notice, most likely added during publication. For every author, such items now sit apart under their own heading, with a note that publishers often add these links and labels, so they do not show that the authors knew. The other citations stay counted, because the reviews were published after the retractions.
changes_since_letter: Every author: an item whose published reference list links the retraction notice or labels the work retracted now sits apart under the heading "The published reference list marks the work as retracted", with a note that publishers often add such links and labels during publication, so they do not show that the authors knew. | Wu L et al. (Cell Biol Int) left out under the rule for retractions that do not touch the results (a missing copyright form), so his 2022 review on retinoblastoma is no longer counted. | Timelines printed beside two reviews: his 2021 Mol Ther Oncolytics review (no submission date available; online 22 Dec 2021, after the cited works were retracted between July and November 2021) and his 2024 Cell Mol Life Sci review (submitted 2 Jul 2023, before the retraction of 11 Aug 2023). | Xie P et al. (Cancer Biomark 2017): our letter gave the retraction year as 2022; the page gives the notice's year, 2023, with its online date (11 Dec 2022). | The page now notes that his 2023 Front Oncol review was itself retracted (Sep 2026), after an expression of concern in Jan 2026. | His entry: from 10 papers and 35 citations in our letter to 9 papers and 34 citations, all in reviews.

summary: In two replies, Dr Moghbeli confirms that the citations are correct. He says each review was finished and first submitted before the cited papers were retracted. In his second reply he adds that the six reviews were submitted, rejected and passed from journal to journal over long periods, often through Springer's transfer to the next journal it suggested, and that the retractions came during those transfers. Once a manuscript is under review, authors cannot change it unless the journal sends it back, and journals did not then check references for retractions as they do now; so he says authors cannot find such references unless the journal checks them and asks for a correction, and that such citations are inevitable in reviews with hundreds of references that pass through several journals. He says the retracted references, 11 of the 1,546 in the seven reviews, have no significant negative effect on the reviews' topics or conclusions. He also said the first item, Roberts JT et al. (Ann Oncol 2006), is not retracted and has no retraction notice.
quote: When we wrote, prepared, and submitted these review manuscripts, the cited papers were not yet retracted.
our_response: The record he checked is the original 2005 trial in J Clin Oncol, which is not retracted; the Ann Oncol 2006 paper was retracted in 2011 as a redundant publication of it, and had already been left out under the rule for duplicates. His timelines match the journal records and the notices and are printed beside each review; those citations stay counted, because the reviews were published after the retractions. His second reply explains how the manuscripts moved between journals; it changes no entry.
changes_since_letter: Roberts JT et al. (Ann Oncol 2006) is left out (retracted in 2011 as a redundant publication of results that stay published in J Clin Oncol), so his 2020 Cell Commun Signal review is not counted. | Timelines printed beside the six remaining reviews: first-submission dates from his account, the rest from the journal records and the retraction notices. | His entry: from 7 papers and 11 citations in our letter to 6 papers and 10 citations, all in reviews.

entry: Rubio D et al., Cancer Res 2005
summary: Dr Bernad says the 2005 paper was the first report of an apparent spontaneous transformation of mesenchymal stem cells in culture, at a time when these cells were being tested in many cell therapies, so it had a large impact on the field. Soon after publication his group found that the main conclusion could not be reproduced and was most probably due to a very small number of contaminating transformed cells that overgrew the cultures. He says the group contacted Cancer Research to offer a retraction; the journal preferred a short notice to the longer one they wrote (de la Fuente et al., 2010). He says the group approached the journal soon after finding the result could not be reproduced. He did not give the date of that contact by 28 October (the notice was published in August 2010). He proposed a note for later authors, printed below as he wrote it, and points to his group's later work on long-term culture of these cells.
quote: Soon after publication (Rubio et al., 2005) we realized that the main conclusion was non reproducible and that the putative spontaneous transformation was most probably due to a highly minoritarian number of a transformed cell line.
statement: Please, be aware that the main conclusion of the manuscript (Rubio et al., 2005) was non-reproducible and that the putative spontaneous transformation of MSC, upon in vitro culture, was most probably due to a highly minoritarian number of contaminant- transformed cells, that with time overgrow the cultures. Then it was retracted (de la Fuente et al., 2010). Therefore, continue citing this work as a proof of the potential of MSC to be transformed upon prolonged in vitro culture, is no appropriate and can induce more confusion to the field
our_response: The retraction notice was published in Cancer Research in August 2010 (doi:10.1158/0008-5472.CAN-10-2451). His group's later papers: Estrada JC et al., Cell Death Dis 2013 (replicative senescence of these cells in long-term culture is closely linked to aneuploidy) and Sepúlveda JC et al., Stem Cells 2014 (senescence abrogates their therapeutic potential in a mouse model of lethal endotoxemia). The entry stands: the citations counted were made after the retraction and use the paper as support.
changes_since_letter: Reason changed from the Retraction Watch group "error or unreliable results" to the notice's wording: the authors could not reproduce some of the transformation events and suspect a cross-contamination artifact; five of the seven authors agreed to the retraction. | Citations judged: from 135 in our letter to 134. One citing paper, which only mentions the work in passing, was published online on 13 July 2010, before the retraction, and is left out; the 33 citations that use it as support are unchanged. | 23 Oct 2026: a check of the citing papers' full text found 3 of the 33 citations in our letter were not cited as support (two warn readers about the retraction, one credits the paper with something it does not report). A full-text check of the other 30 the same day kept 26: two more warn readers and two more credit the paper with something it does not report. Because every paper near the last places was read in full, the paper stays on the list, at place 8 with 26.
